slides.title: Measuring the Motor's Speed
slides.subtitle: ENGS 28 · Day 12 — In-Class

slides.title: Where we are
items: On Wednesday we worked through TTmotor_ramp.c one register at a time.
In the reading you worked out how to turn a count of pulses from the speed sensor into revolutions per minute.
Today we'll wire that sensor, look at its output on the oscilloscope, and then build the rest of the Lab 6 system with the measurement in it.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min, out of a 6-minute bucket that also covers the two transitions into and out of the build. 110 minutes today: 6 settling and transitions, Parts of 8 / 26 / 15 / 8 / 5, 37 for the build with a floor of 30, and 5 for the close. Ask everyone to get the motor setup out now.

slides.title: Wire the sensor and look at its output
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 26 min, and this is the Part that can eat the hour — it is the only one gated on hardware working for everybody at once. Before anything else: take the scope and the multimeter off Wednesday's PWM node and go back to the bare circuit. Order matters — predict FIRST, then wire, then the states figure. The pull-up never gets cut for time. Her slide 5's standard, and it is the one to hold to: nobody leaves today without pulses on their screen. Groups that get a trace early can start counting the slots on their wheel, which is Part 3's first task.

slides.title: Predict: what will the trace look like?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min. Collect two or three answers and write them on the board without ruling on any of them. Say the second bullet out loud — the picture on this slide HAS the resistor in it, and the prediction is about the circuit without it. Do NOT say what the pull-up is for: sl-day12-states is the reveal.

slides.title: Wire the sensor
The photointerrupter on a cable
Wire it, scope it, and measure the pulse rate
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 15 min, of which the last is in hand for the tables that finish early — send them to count the slots on their wheel, which is Part 3's first task. That is Part 2's 26th minute and the first thing to drop if this runs to 30. Turning the wheel by hand is the check to insist on before the motor is started: it is the only test where the student controls the input. Watch for tables with nothing on the screen and send them to the trace table.

slides.title: What the trace is telling you
Why the output needs a pull-up
Why 3.3 V, and why about 10 kΩ
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min. This is the one they have not had before — Day 3 and Day 10 both gave them pull-ups without a value argument. Do not turn it into a calculation; it is a trade-off with a wide middle, which is why 10 kΩ answers a lot of these questions. Bullets 2 and 3 are no longer in the in-class prose — they live in subsec-motors-ref-sensor now, so point the room there rather than at this Part.

slides.title: The complete Lab 6 system
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 1 min. Her slide 10. The picture's job is the block layout — do NOT ask them to read pin names off it, because the Nucleo silkscreen in this image is far too small to project. Every pin name they need is on the build-order slide as text. Point at the four blocks and the two supplies, and move on. Say the inventory out loud while it is up: the driver (motor_init/motor_mode/motor_speed) is theirs to write from Wednesday's TTmotor_ramp.c; start_conversion() and adc_read() they have from Day 7; SevenSeg_number() and the signed counter are Day 10's, and the signed counter was homework nobody reviewed — tell them to check it tonight rather than on the evening the lab is due.

Where you are, and what is left
items: You have the speed sensor wired, its pulses on the oscilloscope, and the arithmetic that turns them into revolutions per minute.
For Lab 6: the tb6612 driver, the potentiometer mapped to a mode and a speed, the pulse counter on PA15, and the rpm on the display.
The optional experiment at the end of the lab is the 50 Hz one: run the PWM at 50 Hz instead of 1.6 kHz and listen to the motor.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 5 min, protected — stop the build for it whatever state the room is in. One minute individual and written first: the stage number you reached, and the first thing you will do tonight. Then round the TABLES, not the individuals — about six tables at fifteen seconds. Then the two items above. The private note before the public round is the difference between a checkpoint and a roll call for a student who is behind. Ask the tables who never got a trace to say so: her standard for today is that nobody leaves without pulses on their screen.
